name: Write and tune a Falco rule
objective: CKS › Runtime Security (the behavioral-detection slice the exam weights heavily). Drill every Falco corner harder than the exam: deploy the DaemonSet with the right driver, confirm the per-node rollout, author a custom rule with exact macros, shape its output fields, reuse a list + macro, tune with an exception, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix of a broken rule. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Custom rule: shell in a container (exact macros)
questions.teach:
A Falco `- rule:` needs `rule:`, `desc:`, `condition:`, `output:`, `priority:`. Reuse Falco's **macros** in the condition: `spawned_process` (an exec), `container` (in a container), `shell_procs` (bash/sh/zsh). Put custom rules in **`falco_rules.local.yaml`** (the `falco` ConfigMap key), never the shipped `falco_rules.yaml`.

**Gotcha:** name it exactly `Terminal shell in container` and set `priority: WARNING` — the grader checks both.
questions.prompt:
Add a custom rule named exactly `Terminal shell in container` to the `falco` ConfigMap's `falco_rules.local.yaml`. Its `condition` must reference `spawned_process`, `container`, and `shell_procs`, and its `priority` must be `WARNING`.

Target: that rule block exists with the three macros in its condition and priority WARNING.
questions.hint:
Edit the ConfigMap key `falco_rules.local.yaml`:
```
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
```
then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
questions.solution:
# Edit the 'falco' ConfigMap, under data.falco_rules.local.yaml, append:
cat <<'EOF'
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
EOF
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco

verification.description: rule 'Terminal shell in container' present with condition macros + priority WARNING

questions.eli5:
Imagine your container is a house, and Falco is a **security guard** watching the front door. The guard doesn't stop anyone — it just **shouts an alert** when it sees something it's been told to watch for.

A **rule** is the guard's instruction card. Each card must say five things: what to call this situation (`rule:`), a human note about it (`desc:`), *when* to shout (`condition:`), *what* to shout (`output:`), and *how loud* (`priority:`).

Writing conditions from scratch is tedious, so Falco ships pre-written shorthand phrases called **macros**. Instead of spelling out "a program was just launched," you write `spawned_process`. Instead of "this is happening inside a container," you write `container`. And `shell_procs` means "the program is a shell like bash/sh/zsh." Chain them with `and`: *someone launched a shell inside a container* = `spawned_process and container and shell_procs`. That's almost always a human poking around where they shouldn't be.

You write your own cards in a **separate notebook** called `falco_rules.local.yaml`, never in Falco's shipped `falco_rules.yaml` (an upgrade would overwrite your work there).

**Watch out for:**

- Put custom rules in **`falco_rules.local.yaml`** (the `falco` ConfigMap key), **never** the shipped `falco_rules.yaml` — upgrades clobber it.
- The grader checks the name **exactly**: `Terminal shell in container`. Wrong case or spacing fails.
- `priority:` must be **`WARNING`** here — it's required, not optional.
- All five keys (`rule`, `desc`, `condition`, `output`, `priority`) must be present or Falco rejects the rule.
- After editing the ConfigMap you must **reload Falco** (`kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`) — it reads rules at startup.
questions.deepDive:
## Writing a custom Falco rule — full rundown

### Mental model
Falco is a **runtime detection** engine: it taps the kernel's syscall stream (via eBPF or a kernel module), matches each event against a set of **rules**, and emits an **alert** when a rule's `condition` is true. It detects; it does not block (that is `seccomp`/AppArmor/admission's job). A rule is "if this syscall pattern happens, shout this message at this severity."

### Anatomy of a rule
Every `- rule:` entry needs five keys:

| Key | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `rule` | ✅ | Unique human name (also the alert's rule name) |
| `desc` | ✅ | One-line description of what it detects |
| `condition` | ✅ | Boolean filter over event fields/macros — when to fire |
| `output` | ✅ | The alert string, with `%`-interpolated fields |
| `priority` | ✅ | Severity: `EMERGENCY` > `ALERT` > `CRITICAL` > `ERROR` > `WARNING` > `NOTICE` > `INFORMATIONAL` > `DEBUG` |
| `tags` | optional | Labels for grouping/filtering (e.g. `[container, shell, mitre_execution]`) |
| `enabled` | optional | `true` by default; `false` disables the rule |

```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell, mitre_execution]
```

### Macros — reusable condition fragments
A **macro** is a named, reusable `condition:` snippet. Falco's default ruleset ships many; you compose them with `and`/`or`/`not`:

| Macro | Expands to (roughly) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spawned_process` | `evt.type in (execve, execveat) and evt.dir=<` | a process was just exec'd |
| `container` | `container.id != host` | event happened inside a container, not on the host |
| `shell_procs` | `proc.name in (shell_binaries)` | the process is a shell (bash, sh, zsh, …) |

`spawned_process and container and shell_procs` = "a shell was exec'd inside a container" — the canonical `Terminal shell in container` rule.

### Where custom rules live
```
/etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml         # shipped defaults — DO NOT edit (upgrades overwrite)
/etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml   # YOUR custom + override rules
/etc/falco/rules.d/*.yaml           # additional drop-in dir
```
In the Helm/DaemonSet install these are keys in the **`falco` ConfigMap**. Add custom rules under the `falco_rules.local.yaml` key. Load order matters: later files **override** earlier rules of the same name, which is how you tune the shipped ruleset without touching it.

### Commands
```bash
# inspect the configmap
kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o yaml

# edit the local rules key
kubectl -n falco edit configmap falco

# validate rules syntax offline (inside a falco pod / with the binary)
falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml

# apply changes — Falco reads rules at startup, so restart the DaemonSet
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
kubectl -n falco rollout status  ds/falco
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Edit `falco_rules.local.yaml`, never `falco_rules.yaml`.** The shipped file is replaced on every upgrade; your custom rules there vanish.
- **Exact name match.** The grader (and overrides) key on the `rule:` string — `Terminal shell in container`, exact case/spacing.
- **`priority` is mandatory** and must be a valid level; this lab requires `WARNING`.
- **A syntax error in one rule fails the whole file** — Falco refuses to load it, silently blinding detection. Check pod logs for load errors.
- **Rules are read at startup only** — after any ConfigMap change you must `rollout restart` the DaemonSet (or rely on hot-reload if configured) or the change does nothing.
- An undefined macro referenced in a condition is a load error, not a silent skip.

### Quick reference
```yaml
# falco_rules.local.yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
```
```bash
kubectl -n falco edit configmap falco          # add under falco_rules.local.yaml
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco       # reload
```

questions.title: Shape the alert output fields
questions.teach:
An alert is only useful if the **`output:`** string carries context. Falco interpolates `%`-fields: `%user.name` (who), `%container.id`/`%container.name` (where), `%proc.cmdline` (what ran), `%evt.time` (when). You compose them into a human-readable line.

**Gotcha:** fields are prefixed with `%` and must be spelled exactly — a typo like `%proc.cmd` silently renders as the literal text, not the value.
questions.prompt:
Make the `Terminal shell in container` rule's `output:` carry full context: it must include the fields `%user.name`, `%container.id`, and `%proc.cmdline`.

Target: the rule's `output` string references all three of `%user.name`, `%container.id`, and `%proc.cmdline`.
questions.hint: Set the rule's `output:` to e.g. `"Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"`. Keep the `%` prefix and exact field names.
questions.solution:
# In the same rule, ensure output references all three fields:
#   output: "Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
questions.eli5:
An alert that just says *"something happened!"* is useless at 3 a.m. — you need to know **who** did **what**, **where**. That's the job of the rule's **`output:`** line: it's the sentence the security guard actually shouts.

Think of it like a fill-in-the-blanks incident report. Falco gives you little placeholders that start with a **`%`**, and at alert time it swaps each one for the real value it saw:

- `%user.name` — *who* did it (the username)
- `%container.id` — *where* it happened (which container)
- `%proc.cmdline` — *what* they actually typed/ran

So you write a template like `Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)`, and Falco turns it into `Shell in container (user=root container=a1b2c3 cmd=/bin/bash -i)`.

The catch: Falco only substitutes a placeholder if it **exactly recognises** the field name. There's no spell-check.

**Watch out for:**

- Every field **must start with `%`** and be spelled **exactly** — `%proc.cmdline`, not `%proc.cmd` or `proc.cmdline`.
- A **typo renders as literal text**, silently: `%proc.cmd` just prints the characters "%proc.cmd" instead of the command. No error — you only notice when the alert looks wrong.
- The grader needs **all three** fields present: `%user.name`, `%container.id`, **and** `%proc.cmdline`.
- Wrap the whole thing in quotes in YAML, since it contains spaces and special characters.
- After editing, **reload Falco** (`kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`) for the new output to take effect.
questions.deepDive:
## Shaping Falco alert output fields — full rundown

### Mental model
The `condition` decides **whether** a rule fires; the **`output`** decides **what the alert says**. Output is a template string where `%`-prefixed tokens are **output fields** that Falco resolves from the triggering event at fire time. A good output answers *who / what / where / when* so a responder can act without re-deriving context.

### Field syntax
- Every field is prefixed with **`%`**: `%user.name`.
- Fields come from the same classes you filter on in conditions (`proc.*`, `user.*`, `container.*`, `fd.*`, `evt.*`, `k8s.*`).
- Literal text around fields is printed verbatim; add `key=` labels so output is greppable.
- Quote the whole string in YAML when it contains spaces/parentheses.

### Commonly-used output fields
| Field | Answers | Example value |
|---|---|---|
| `%user.name` | who (username) | `root` |
| `%user.uid` | who (numeric uid) | `0` |
| `%proc.name` | what process | `bash` |
| `%proc.cmdline` | what command + args | `/bin/bash -i` |
| `%proc.pname` | parent process | `runc` |
| `%container.id` | where (short container id) | `a1b2c3d4e5f6` |
| `%container.name` | where (container name) | `web` |
| `%container.image.repository` | which image | `nginx` |
| `%fd.name` | which file/socket | `/etc/shadow` |
| `%evt.type` | which syscall | `execve` |
| `%evt.time` | when | `12:01:02.000` |
| `%k8s.ns.name` / `%k8s.pod.name` | k8s context | `prod` / `web-xyz` |

### How resolution works
At fire time Falco walks the output string and replaces each recognised `%field` with its value. An **unrecognised field name is NOT substituted** — it is emitted as the literal characters. There is no validation error, so a typo degrades silently.

```yaml
output: "Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
# renders:  Shell in container (user=root container=a1b2c3d4 cmd=/bin/bash -i)

output: "cmd=%proc.cmd"       # typo
# renders:  cmd=%proc.cmd      <-- literal, silently wrong
```

### Verifying a field name
```bash
# list every supported output/filter field
falco --list
falco --list | grep -i cmdline        # confirm %proc.cmdline exists
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`%` prefix is mandatory** on every field in the output; without it the token is plain text.
- **Typos render literally, no error** — `%proc.cmd`, `%container.name2`, `%usr.name` all print as text. Always confirm against `falco --list`.
- Output fields and **condition** fields are the same namespace — if you can filter on it you can print it.
- This step requires **all three**: `%user.name`, `%container.id`, `%proc.cmdline`. Missing one fails the grader even if the alert still fires.
- Changing only `output` still requires a **rollout restart** (or hot-reload) to take effect.
- `%container.id` is empty/`host` for host-side events — fine here because the condition already includes the `container` macro.

### Quick reference
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
```
```bash
falco --list | grep -E 'user.name|container.id|proc.cmdline'   # verify field names
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco                       # reload
```

questions.title: Reuse a list + macro
questions.teach:
Falco lets you factor conditions: a **`- list:`** is a named set of values (`items: [a, b]`) and a **`- macro:`** is a named reusable `condition:`. You reference a list with `in (list_name)` and a macro by name. This keeps rules DRY and readable.

**Gotcha:** a list is referenced as `field in (list_name)` — the parentheses are required; writing `field in list_name` is a syntax error.
questions.prompt:
In `falco_rules.local.yaml` add BOTH:
- a **list** named `sensitive_dirs` with items `/etc` and `/root`
- a **macro** named `write_sensitive_dir` whose condition is `evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs)`

Target: a `- list: sensitive_dirs` containing /etc and /root, and a `- macro: write_sensitive_dir` that references `sensitive_dirs`.
questions.hint:
```
- list: sensitive_dirs
  items: [/etc, /root]
- macro: write_sensitive_dir
  condition: (evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs))
```
then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF'
- list: sensitive_dirs
  items: [/etc, /root]
- macro: write_sensitive_dir
  condition: (evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs))
EOF
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
questions.eli5:
Imagine you're writing lots of guard instructions, and the same long phrase keeps showing up: "the list of folders we care about is /etc and /root." Copy-pasting that everywhere is tiring and error-prone. Falco gives you two tools to avoid repeating yourself — like saving things as reusable sticky notes.

- A **list** is a named bag of values. `sensitive_dirs` = the bag holding `/etc` and `/root`. Write it once, refer to it by name forever.
- A **macro** is a named reusable *condition* — a saved phrase. `write_sensitive_dir` = "a file in one of our sensitive dirs is being opened." Now any rule can just say `write_sensitive_dir` instead of spelling out the whole test.

To check whether something is *in* a list, you write `field in (list_name)` — with the value `pmatch (sensitive_dirs)` meaning "does this path start with any entry in the bag." The key detail: **the parentheses around the list name are required.**

This keeps rules short, readable, and easy to update — change the list in one place and every rule using it updates.

**Watch out for:**

- A list is referenced as `field in (list_name)` — the **parentheses are mandatory**. `field in list_name` is a **syntax error** that fails the whole file to load.
- A **list** holds values (`items: [/etc, /root]`); a **macro** holds a condition. Don't mix them up.
- `pmatch` means "path prefix match" — good for directories; it's different from plain `in` (exact match).
- The macro's condition here is `evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs)` — note `in (open,openat)` also needs its parentheses.
- Defining a list/macro does nothing on its own until a rule references it — and you must **reload Falco** afterwards.
questions.deepDive:
## Falco lists & macros — full rundown

### Mental model
Falco rule files have three top-level item kinds: **`- rule:`**, **`- macro:`**, and **`- list:`**. Lists and macros exist to keep conditions **DRY** and readable — define a value set or a condition fragment once, reference it by name in many rules. This is exactly how Falco's own default ruleset is built.

| Item | Holds | Referenced as |
|---|---|---|
| `- list:` | a set of literal values (`items:`) | `field in (list_name)` / `field pmatch (list_name)` |
| `- macro:` | a reusable `condition:` fragment | by its name, inside another condition |
| `- rule:` | a full detection (condition+output+priority) | n/a (it fires) |

### Lists
```yaml
- list: sensitive_dirs
  items: [/etc, /root]
```
- `items` is a YAML sequence of literal values (flow `[a, b]` or block form).
- Reference a list **only** inside parentheses after an operator:
  - `fd.name in (sensitive_dirs)` — exact membership
  - `fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs)` — **path-prefix** match (matches `/etc`, `/etc/passwd`, `/root/.ssh`, …)
- Lists can contain other lists (nested expansion).

### Macros
```yaml
- macro: write_sensitive_dir
  condition: (evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs))
```
- A macro's value is a `condition:` fragment — any boolean expression.
- Wrap the macro body in parentheses as a habit so operator precedence is preserved when it is `and`/`or`-combined into a larger rule.
- Use it in a rule by name:
  ```yaml
  - rule: Write below sensitive dir
    desc: file opened for write under /etc or /root
    condition: write_sensitive_dir and container
    output: "sensitive write (file=%fd.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
    priority: WARNING
  ```

### Operators that take a list
| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `in (list)` | value equals one of the list entries (exact) |
| `pmatch (list)` | value's path matches/has-prefix one of the list entries |
| `intersects (list)` | any overlap (for multi-value fields) |
| `glob` | shell-style glob match (single pattern, not a list) |

**Parentheses are required** around the list name for `in`, `pmatch`, `intersects` — and around inline value sets like `in (open, openat)`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`field in list_name` (no parens) is a syntax error** → Falco refuses to load the whole file. Always `in (list_name)`.
- **`pmatch` ≠ `in`.** `pmatch` is prefix/path matching (right for directories); `in` is exact equality. For `/etc`-style dir rules use `pmatch`.
- A **list holds values**, a **macro holds a condition** — swapping them (putting a condition in `items:`, or values in a macro `condition:`) fails validation.
- Order/append matters only for overrides of same-named items; a list/macro must be **defined** (same file or a loaded file) before/with the rule that uses it, or you get an "undefined" load error.
- Defining a list/macro changes nothing until a **rule references it** and Falco is reloaded (`rollout restart ds/falco`).
- Inline value sets also need parens: `evt.type in (open,openat)`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
- list: sensitive_dirs
  items: [/etc, /root]

- macro: write_sensitive_dir
  condition: (evt.type in (open,openat) and fd.name pmatch (sensitive_dirs))
```
```bash
falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml   # catch missing-parens / undefined errors
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
```

questions.title: Tune the rule with an exception
questions.teach:
Known-good activity (a health-check binary) causes false positives. **Tune**, don't delete: add an `exceptions:` list on the rule — each entry has `name:`, `fields:`, optional `comps:`, and `values:`. A match in any exception makes the rule **not** fire. (Alternatively, `and not <macro>` the condition.)

**Gotcha:** `fields`, `comps`, and `values` must line up positionally, and `in`-style values are bracket-wrapped, e.g. `values: - [my-healthcheck]`.
questions.prompt:
Tune `Terminal shell in container` so a process named `my-healthcheck` does NOT fire it. Add an `exceptions:` entry named `known_good` on the rule that lists `proc.name` and references `my-healthcheck` (or add a macro and `and not ...` it into the condition).

Target: the rule has an exception named `known_good` (or a tuning macro) referencing `my-healthcheck`.
questions.hint:
Under the rule add:
```
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps: [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
```
then `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.
questions.solution:
# Append to the 'Terminal shell in container' rule:
cat <<'EOF'
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps: [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
EOF
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
questions.eli5:
Your "shell in a container" alarm works great — but there's one program, a **health-check** that your own system runs constantly, that keeps setting it off. It's totally harmless, but now the guard cries wolf every few seconds, and real alerts drown in the noise.

The rookie move is to **delete the rule** to stop the noise. Don't! Then you're blind to the *actual* bad shells too. Instead you **tune** it: tell the guard "this one specific thing is fine, ignore it, but keep watching for everything else."

Falco's way to do that is an **`exceptions:`** list attached to the rule. You give the exception a name (`known_good`), say which fact to check (`proc.name`), how to compare it (`in`), and the allowed value (`my-healthcheck`). If an event matches an exception, the rule **does not fire** — but every other shell still trips it.

Think of it as a VIP "do-not-alarm" wristband for one trusted program, instead of switching the alarm off.

(There's also an older style: add `and not <a macro matching my-healthcheck>` to the condition. Same effect.)

**Watch out for:**

- **Tune, don't delete.** Removing the rule blinds you to real threats; an exception keeps detection alive.
- In an exception, **`fields`, `comps`, and `values` must line up positionally** — the 1st field uses the 1st comp against the 1st values entry.
- `in`-style values are **bracket-wrapped**: `values:` then `- [my-healthcheck]` (a list inside the list).
- Give the exception a `name:` — here it must reference `my-healthcheck` and the grader looks for `known_good` (or an equivalent tuning macro).
- The alternative `and not <macro>` approach is valid too, but keep it readable.
- Reload Falco after editing (`kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`).
questions.deepDive:
## Tuning a Falco rule with exceptions — full rundown

### Mental model
Real environments generate **benign** activity that matches your rule (health checks, backup agents, CI runners). The goal is to suppress *those specific* events **without** weakening detection of everything else. Two supported approaches:

1. **`exceptions:`** — a structured, per-rule allow-list (preferred, modern).
2. **`and not <macro>`** — fold a negated condition into the rule.

Never "fix" a false positive by deleting the rule or setting `enabled: false` — that blinds the whole detection.

### The `exceptions:` structure
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.id cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps:  [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
```

Each exception item:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | unique label for this exception (required) |
| `fields` | ordered list of event fields to test |
| `comps` | ordered list of comparison operators, **positionally aligned** with `fields` (default `=`) |
| `values` | the value tuples; an event matching any tuple is **excluded** (rule won't fire) |

Semantics: an exception adds, implicitly, `and not (field comp value ...)` to the condition. If **any** exception matches, the rule is suppressed for that event.

### Positional alignment (the tricky part)
`fields`, `comps`, and `values` tuples line up **by index**:
```yaml
  exceptions:
  - name: hc
    fields: [proc.name, proc.pname]
    comps:  [in,        =]
    values:
    - [[my-healthcheck, curl], runc]   # proc.name in (my-healthcheck,curl) AND proc.pname = runc
```
- Single field + `in`: the value is a **bracket-wrapped set**: `- [my-healthcheck]` (or `- [[my-healthcheck, other]]` for the multi-field form where that slot is itself a set).
- Omit `comps` to default every field to `=`.

### Alternative: `and not <macro>`
```yaml
- macro: is_healthcheck
  condition: proc.name = my-healthcheck

- rule: Terminal shell in container
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs and not is_healthcheck
  ...
```
Functionally equivalent; `exceptions:` is cleaner for append-style tuning and is what the ecosystem standardises on.

### Appending vs overriding (advanced)
In newer Falco you can **append** an exception to an existing shipped rule rather than redefining it:
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps: [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
  override:
    exceptions: append      # merge into the existing rule's exceptions
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`fields` / `comps` / `values` must align positionally** — a misaligned comp silently changes meaning or fails validation.
- **`in` values are bracket-wrapped** — `- [my-healthcheck]`, not `- my-healthcheck`.
- Each exception needs a **`name`**; here it must be `known_good` (or a tuning macro that references `my-healthcheck`).
- An exception **suppresses matching events only** — the rule still fires for every non-excepted shell. That's the point: tune, don't disable.
- **Do not** set `enabled: false` or delete the rule to kill a false positive — that is the anti-pattern this step tests against.
- Reload after editing: `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
  exceptions:
  - name: known_good
    fields: [proc.name]
    comps:  [in]
    values:
    - [my-healthcheck]
```
```bash
falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
```

questions.title: Keep the rule enabled
questions.teach:
A Falco `- rule:` is **enabled by default**. An explicit `enabled: false` on the rule block (or commenting it out) silently stops detection even on a perfectly healthy DaemonSet — a classic way to accidentally blind your monitoring.

**Gotcha:** `enabled:` lives on the rule block itself; there's no cluster-wide toggle — each rule carries its own state.

questions.eli5:
You've built a great alarm. Now the sneaky question: is it actually **switched on**?

Every Falco rule has a hidden on/off switch called `enabled`. The good news is it defaults to **on** — you don't have to write anything to keep a rule working. The trap is the opposite: if someone slips `enabled: false` onto the rule, or comments the whole rule out with `#`, the DaemonSet keeps running perfectly, the pods are all healthy and green... and the rule quietly detects **nothing**. It's an alarm with the battery secretly removed — looks fine, protects nothing.

There's no master switch for the whole cluster, either. Each rule carries its **own** on/off state. So "is detection live?" has to be checked rule by rule.

For this step the job is simple: make sure `Terminal shell in container` is a real, active `- rule:` entry (not commented out) and does **not** have `enabled: false` hanging off it.

**Watch out for:**

- `enabled: false` on a rule **silently disables it** even though the DaemonSet looks perfectly healthy — a classic way to accidentally blind monitoring.
- **Commenting the rule out** (`#`) has the same effect — it's no longer loaded.
- There is **no cluster-wide enable toggle** — `enabled` lives on each rule block individually.
- A rule is **enabled by default**; you only need to *remove* `enabled: false`, not add `enabled: true` (though adding it is harmless).
- After re-enabling, **reload Falco** (`kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`) so it picks up the change.
- "Healthy pods" is not the same as "detecting" — green status never proves a rule is live.
questions.deepDive:
## Keeping a Falco rule enabled — full rundown

### Mental model
A Falco rule's **state** (enabled/disabled) is a property of the **rule block itself**, not a cluster or DaemonSet setting. A perfectly healthy Falco DaemonSet with every pod Ready will still detect **nothing** for a rule that is disabled or commented out. "Running" ≠ "detecting." Verifying enablement is part of operating runtime security correctly.

### The `enabled` field
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: ...
  condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
  output: "..."
  priority: WARNING
  enabled: true        # default — rule is active even if omitted
```
- **Default is `true`** — a rule with no `enabled:` key is active.
- `enabled: false` turns the rule **off** while leaving it in the file (loaded but inert).
- **Commenting out** the `- rule:` block with `#` also disables it (it's simply not parsed).

### Three ways a rule ends up silently off
| Cause | Looks like | Detection |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled: false` on the block | rule present in file | ❌ off |
| Entire block commented `#- rule:` | rule text in file as comments | ❌ off |
| A later override sets `enabled: false` | first definition looks fine | ❌ off (override wins) |

All three leave the DaemonSet green and give no runtime error — the dangerous part.

### Enabling via override (modern pattern)
To toggle a shipped rule without redefining it, newer Falco supports:
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  enabled: true
  override:
    enabled: replace
```

### Verifying what is actually loaded
```bash
# dump the rules key and look for the rule + any enabled:false
kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o jsonpath='{.data.falco_rules\.local\.yaml}'

# at the binary level, list loaded rules
falco --list-rules            # (version-dependent) rules Falco actually loaded

# confirm no load errors / disabled notices in logs
kubectl -n falco logs ds/falco | grep -iE 'rule|error|disabled'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`enabled: false` is silent** — no error, pods stay Ready, detection is off. A classic "blinded monitoring" trap.
- **Commenting the block out** has the identical effect; check for a leading `#`.
- **There is no global enable switch** — each rule carries its own `enabled` state; you cannot toggle them all at once.
- A rule is **enabled by default**, so the fix is to *remove* `enabled: false` (or set it `true`) — you don't need to add `enabled: true` to a rule that never had the flag.
- Beware **override order**: a later same-named rule can flip `enabled`, so the effective state is whatever loads last.
- Changes require a **reload**: `kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  # ...condition/output/priority...
  # NO 'enabled: false'  →  active by default
```
```bash
kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o jsonpath='{.data.falco_rules\.local\.yaml}' | grep -n enabled
kubectl -n falco rollout restart ds/falco
```
